exercises.prompt: Implement doubleAll(arr) so it returns a new array in which every number from arr has been multiplied by 2. An empty array returns an empty array.
hints: arr.map(fn) builds a brand-new array by running fn on each element — exactly the 'transform every item' shape.
The transform is a doubling: x => x * 2.
map already handles the empty array — mapping over [] returns [] — so you need no special case.

exercises.prompt: Implement sumEven(arr) so it returns the sum of only the even numbers in arr. An empty array, or one with no even numbers, returns 0.
hints: Declare an accumulator at 0 before the loop, then add to it as you find even numbers.
x % 2 === 0 tests evenness, and it holds for negatives and zero too (-4 and 0 are both even).
Return the accumulator after the loop — if nothing was even it is still 0, which is also the empty-array answer.

exercises.prompt: Implement countVowels(str) so it returns how many vowels (a, e, i, o, u) the string contains, counting both uppercase and lowercase. An empty string returns 0.
hints: Lowercase the whole string first with str.toLowerCase() so 'A' and 'a' count the same.
Walk the characters with a for...of loop and test each one against the vowels.
'aeiou'.includes(ch) is a compact membership test — increment a counter each time it is true.

exercises.prompt: Implement longerThan(words, minLength) so it returns a new array holding only the strings from words whose length is strictly greater than minLength, in their original order. A word exactly minLength characters long is left out. An empty array — or one where nothing is long enough — returns an empty array.
hints: Keeping some elements and dropping the rest is the filter shape — the result may be shorter than the input, and the survivors stay in their original order.
A string's length is w.length, and 'strictly greater' means > rather than >=, so a word exactly minLength long is dropped.
return words.filter(w => w.length > minLength) — filtering an empty array already gives [], so no special case is needed.

exercises.prompt: Implement parityLabels(arr) so it returns a new array of the same length as arr, holding 'even' for each even number and 'odd' for each odd one — parityLabels([1, 2]) is ['odd', 'even']. Zero is even, and negatives count as well (-4 is even, -3 is odd). An empty array returns an empty array.
hints: One label per number, same length as the input — that is a transform of every element, so map rather than filter.
Test evenness with x % 2 === 0; do not test oddness with x % 2 === 1, because % keeps the sign of the left operand and -3 % 2 is -1, not 1.
return arr.map(x => x % 2 === 0 ? 'even' : 'odd') — mapping an empty array gives [] for free.
